Said once (scene 1): "These rates and prices change, so check the current ones."
- **Insurance as "who pays?" (standard item 3).** One crash, two bills (your car $3,000; another car $2,500), and a three-column table that fills as each policy is chosen: green slip only (you pay $5,500), third-party property (the other car is covered, less an example $700 excess; your $3,000 is yours: you pay $3,700), comprehensive (both covered; you pay the $850 excess). teaching.causalExplanation: First, stamp duty. It's a tax the state government charges when a car changes owners. In New South Wales, for a car up to forty-five thousand dollars, it's three dollars for every hundred dollars of the price, or part of a hundred. So count the hundreds. Fourteen thousand nine hundred and ninety is a hundred and forty-nine full hundreds, with ninety dollars left over. That ninety is part of a hundred, so it counts as a whole hundred. That's a hundred and fifty lots of a hundred dollars, and a hundred and fifty times three dollars is four hundred and fifty dollars of stamp duty. Multiplying a hundred and forty-nine point nine by three gives four hundred and forty-nine seventy. Close, but wrong, because the rule charges every part of a hundred in full. Dearer cars pay more, but only on the dollars above the limit. Above forty-five thousand dollars, the first forty-five thousand costs a fixed thirteen hundred and fifty, and every hundred, or part, above that costs five dollars. Take a forty-eight thousand dollar ute. The part above the limit is three thousand dollars, which is thirty lots of a hundred. Thirty times five is a hundred and fifty. So the duty is thirteen hundred and fifty plus a hundred and fifty, fifteen hundred dollars. Charging the whole price at five dollars a hundred would almost double it, and that's not the rule. Back to the hatchback. Next comes registration, the yearly fee that lets a car use public roads. Here it's an example three hundred and eighty-five dollars, and it depends on the car's weight. But you can't register a car without a CTP green slip. That's compulsory third-party insurance, and it covers people who are injured in a crash. An example green slip here costs seven hundred and eighty dollars, and young drivers usually pay more. Then there's a small fee to transfer the car into your name, forty-two dollars if you do it within fourteen days. All three are compulsory, so they all go into the cost of buying the car.

Take a forty-eight thousand dollar ute. The part above the limit is three thousand dollars, which is thirty lots of a hundred. Thirty times five is a hundred and fifty. So the duty is thirteen hundred and fifty plus a hundred and fifty, fifteen hundred dollars. Charging the whole price at five dollars a hundred would almost double it, and that's not the rule.

scenes.teachingReason: Back to the hatchback. Next comes registration, the yearly fee that lets a car use public roads. Here it's an example three hundred and eighty-five dollars, and it depends on the car's weight. But you can't register a car without a CTP green slip. That's compulsory third-party insurance, and it covers people who are injured in a crash. An example green slip here costs seven hundred and eighty dollars, and young drivers usually pay more. Then there's a small fee to transfer the car into your name, forty-two dollars if you do it within fourteen days. All three are compulsory, so they all go into the cost of buying the car.

scenes.teachingReason: The green slip covers injuries to people. It doesn't fix cars. Say you crash, and there's three thousand dollars of damage to your car, and two and a half thousand to the other driver's. With only a green slip, you pay all fifty-five hundred yourself. Third-party property insurance is optional, and covers damage you do to other people's cars and property. With it, the other car is paid for, less your excess, the part of a claim you pay yourself, say seven hundred dollars. But your own three thousand is still yours, so you pay thirty-seven hundred. Comprehensive insurance is also optional, and it covers your own car as well. Here it's an example sixteen hundred and forty dollars a year, with an eight hundred and fifty dollar excess. After the same crash, you'd pay just the eight hundred and fifty dollars.
